title: A most unusual theatre

paragraphs.text: The city of Leicester in England, a city with a population of fewer than 300,000, has just taken delivery of a theatre whose technical sophistication equals, and may even surpass, the National Theatre in London. Leicester's Curve Theatre is aptly named, and in setting out to create a new kind of performing and theatre-going experience, its architect Rafael Viñoly has given other great theatrical establishments in Britain serious pause for thought. But this is not just an architectural story. When a city this size commits £61m to a single arts building, people take notice. And when the design process, involving one of the world's most celebrated architects, survives not only the usual backlash from protestors but also four changes of council leadership, we see just how important theatre can be to a city's psyche and cultural ambition.

Leicester is a very suitable case for theatrical treatment. In the 1960s, the city supported two vibrant theatres, the Haymarket and the Phoenix. While the Phoenix is still going as an independent cinema, the Haymarket closed in 2006 following financial difficulties. The Curve is billed as the Haymarket's replacement and will also be run by the Leicester Theatre Trust. The opening season includes 'Cinderella: A Musical', and the only performances outside London of 'in-i', the dance piece starring Juliette Binoche and Akram Khan.

The new Curve Theatre's sweeping lines and four-storey glass front crossed with metal face the 147 snooker hall directly opposite. The theatre's architectural design has nothing to do with the very interesting 19th-century architecture around it: the Curve may have end walls of Leicester stock brick, but this is a 21st-century building that challenges the city's unfortunate motto, semper eadem — 'always the same' — and lights the touch-paper for urban regeneration in the centre of this busy, but possibly outdated, place. Perhaps it's time for a change. Leicester, whose textile and shoe industries once gave the city one of the highest per capita earnings levels in Britain, is now generating new economic momentum through engineering and food production.

Despite the Curve's sloping glass frontage — the dominating feature in daylight — Viñoly and his project architect, Nick Gibbs, have delivered a building founded on a successful concept: an inside-out theatre. The Curve has plainly set a new benchmark in terms of how a theatre is perceived, for here the usual demarcations between on-stage and backstage, promenade spaces and operational spaces, actors and audience, have been erased. Imagine a giant, concrete-floored space under a huge, 1,000-tonne horizontal steel frame resting on four legs, from which the building's glass front is hung. Now, in that clear space, imagine two brightly coloured, full-height areas — the main auditorium and the smaller studio theatre — linked by a central block that contains the Curve's massive stage, subsurface storage, and set-lift zone.

Viñoly's architecture delivers two theatres, one with 750 seats, the other with up to 350. Yet this is a theatre where the phrase 'curtain up' applies to a great deal more than the stage. For 'curtains', rather than walls, are all that separate the theatrical, public and operational spaces. And despite weighing 24 tonnes, the lower portions of the side of the main auditorium facing the street can be raised so that passers-by can see stagehands at work. Getting productions in and out of the theatre is also no problem: part of the side of the building lifts up, and the great pantechnicon transporter reverses in across the public floor of the building and passes through the electrically raised section.

Nobody, least of all the actors, escapes this uncompromising inside-outness. The make-up department is an open shelf on the building's back wall and can be seen from the ground floor and the promenade levels of the theatre areas: to get to the stage from their dressing rooms, actors walk across a public section of the ground floor. There is no permanent formal separation between front-of-house and back-of-house, or between creative and operational; much of the process of performance is itself revealed.

And the theatrical potential of the building is considerable, as the various curtains of the stage can be manipulated and stage areas and seating adjusted. This ability, coupled with the fact that the main rehearsal room is the same size as the big main stage, will clearly give the theatre regional pre-eminence and pulling power.

Is this building an original? In terms of British theatre architecture, certainly. But in a broader sense, it repeats aspects of the sweeping formal bravado of Viñoly's Tokyo International Forum and takes its self-dramatizing cue from the Kimmel Center for the Performing Arts in Philadelphia.

The Curve is Viñoly's first completed building in Britain. There are more on the way: a new arts centre in Colchester, a tower in the City of London, and (if the outraged protests die out) a vast carbon-neutral scheme next to Battersea power station, surmounted by a transparent roof and a 1000-foot glass chimney. The Curve, very nearly street-theatre in architectural form, is therefore Viñoly's calculatedly brilliant entrance to the British scene. It is perhaps too clinical in parts, yet is undoubtedly a remarkable building that throws down a serious challenge to the Curve's artistic director, Paul Kerryson. He's got what he wanted, a theatre without boundaries: what will he do with it?

groups.title: The Curve Theatre
content: The Curve Theatre is an inside-out theatre: much of what goes on inside the theatre is {{31}} to the public. This has been achieved through the use of transparent materials for the {{32}} of the exterior and the fact that there are no walls dividing the actor and audience spaces inside. In addition, the bottom part of the main auditorium can be raised to reveal {{33}} activities to people on the street, while a {{34}} vehicle carrying equipment can drive right into the building. For the actors, {{35}} performances will begin as soon as they leave their dressing rooms.

subtitle: From its radically adaptable stage to its public make-up room, Leicester's new theatre rewrites the script for dramatic design
